lessons.title: Program Structure

sections.objectives:
- Understand the basic structure of a Java application.
- Learn the purpose of public class Main and the main method.
- Output text using System.out.println.
sections.explanation:
In Java, every line of executable code must be inside a class. By convention and toolchain requirement, if your file is named `Main.java`, it contains `public class Main`.

The execution starts at the `main` method with the exact signature:
`public static void main(String[] args)`

- `public`: Accessible from anywhere by the JVM.
- `static`: Can be invoked without creating an instance of the class.
- `void`: Does not return any exit code; termination is controlled by exiting or exceptions.
- `String[] args`: Command-line arguments.

To print output to standard out, Java provides `System.out.println()`.
sections.knowledge_checks:
Q: Why must the class be named Main?
A: In Java, a public class must match the name of the file (Main.java).
Q: What does void mean in the main method signature?
A: It means the method does not return a value.
Q: What method prints text with an automatic newline in Java?
A: System.out.println().
sections.common_mistakes:
- Misspelling `String[] args` or forgetting `static`.
- Using single quotes for strings (single quotes are only for single char literals).
- Forgetting the ending semicolon `;`.
sections.recap:
- Java applications enter through `public static void main(String[] args)`.
- Code must reside inside a class matching the filename.

checks.answer: In Java, a public class must match the name of the file (Main.java).

checks.question: What does void mean in the main method signature?
checks.answer: It means the method does not return a value.

lessons.title: Variables and Types

sections.objectives:
- Declare primitive and reference variables.
- Learn int, double, boolean, char, and String.
- Understand the `final` keyword and type casting.
sections.explanation:
Java is strongly typed. Primitive types include `int` (32-bit integer), `double` (64-bit floating point), `boolean` (`true` or `false`), and `char` (single Unicode character in single quotes).

`String` is a reference type representing immutable text.

Use `final` before a variable type to make it an immutable constant:
`final double PI = 3.14159;`

Type casting allows converting between types:
- Widening (automatic): `int` to `double`
- Narrowing (explicit cast): `(int) 3.99` evaluates to `3`
sections.knowledge_checks:
Q: What is the difference between float and double in Java?
A: double has 64 bits of precision while float has 32 bits; double is the default literal type.
Q: How do you declare a constant variable in Java?
A: Prefix the declaration with the final keyword.
Q: What happens when you cast (int) 7.8?
A: It truncates the decimal part, resulting in 7.
sections.common_mistakes:
- Assigning double values directly to int without an explicit cast.
- Using `==` to compare Strings instead of `.equals()`.
sections.recap:
- Primitive types store raw values (`int`, `double`, `boolean`, `char`).
- `final` creates immutable constants.

lessons.title: Input and Output

sections.objectives:
- Read input from standard input using `java.util.Scanner`.
- Format output with `System.out.printf`.
sections.knowledge_checks:
Q: Which class is commonly used for user input in console applications?
A: java.util.Scanner.
Q: What format specifier in printf formats a floating-point number to two decimal places?
A: %.2f.
Q: Why should you be careful when mixing nextInt() and nextLine()?
A: nextInt() does not consume the trailing newline character, leaving it for the subsequent nextLine().
sections.common_mistakes:
- Forgetting `import java.util.Scanner;`.
- Calling `nextInt()` when input is not an integer, throwing `InputMismatchException`.
sections.recap:
- Use `Scanner` with `System.in` for console input.
- `printf` provides C-style string formatting.

lessons.title: Operators

sections.objectives:
- Work with arithmetic, relational, and logical operators.
- Understand integer division versus floating point division.
- Use ternary operators.
sections.explanation:
Java supports standard arithmetic operators: `+`, `-`, `*`, `/`, `%` (modulo).

**Integer division:**
Dividing two integers truncates the decimal: `7 / 2` is `3`. To get `3.5`, at least one operand must be a floating-point number: `7.0 / 2` or `(double) 7 / 2`.

**Logical Operators:**
- `&&`: Logical AND (short-circuiting)
- `||`: Logical OR (short-circuiting)
- `!`: Logical NOT

**Ternary Operator:**
`condition ? valueIfTrue : valueIfFalse`
sections.knowledge_checks:
Q: What is the result of 9 / 2 in Java?
A: 4, because both operands are integers and the fraction is truncated.
Q: What does the % operator return?
A: The remainder of integer division.
Q: What is short-circuit evaluation in &&?
A: If the left operand is false, the right operand is not evaluated.
sections.common_mistakes:
- Expecting `1 / 2` to yield `0.5` instead of `0`.
- Confusing `=` (assignment) with `==` (comparison).
sections.recap:
- Integer division truncates towards zero.
- Ternary operator provides inline conditional expressions.

checks.answer: The remainder of integer division.

checks.answer: If the left operand is false, the right operand is not evaluated.

lessons.title: Conditions

sections.objectives:
- Branch execution using `if`, `else if`, and `else`.
- Switch statements.
- Compare Strings safely using `.equals()`.
sections.knowledge_checks:
Q: Why shouldn't you compare Strings using ==?
A: == compares object memory references, not character content; .equals() compares text content.
Q: Can a switch statement evaluate String variables in modern Java?
A: Yes, since Java 7 switch supports String cases.
Q: What happens if a break statement is omitted in a traditional switch case?
A: Execution falls through to the next case block.
sections.common_mistakes:
- Comparing `str == "hello"` which can randomly evaluate to false for dynamically allocated strings.
- Missing braces causing only the first following statement to be conditional.
sections.recap:
- Use `if-else` for boolean ranges and `switch` for distinct values.
- Always use `a.equals(b)` for string equality.

lessons.title: Loops

sections.objectives:
- Master `for`, `while`, and `do-while` loops.
- Use `break` and `continue`.
- Understand enhanced for-each loops.
sections.knowledge_checks:
Q: When is a do-while loop preferred over a while loop?
A: When the body must execute at least once before checking the condition.
Q: What does the continue keyword do?
A: It jumps directly to the next iteration of the surrounding loop.
Q: What is an off-by-one error?
A: A loop iterating one time too few or too many due to < vs <= boundary confusion.
sections.common_mistakes:
- Creating accidental infinite loops by forgetting to increment loop counters.
- Semicolon immediately after `for(...) ;` making the body empty.
sections.recap:
- `for` is best for counting iterations.
- `while` is best when the stopping condition is dynamic.

lessons.title: Methods

sections.objectives:
- Define reusable static methods.
- Pass parameters and return values.
- Method overloading.
sections.knowledge_checks:
Q: What allows multiple methods in the same class to share the same name?
A: Method overloading, provided their parameter types or counts differ.
Q: Are arguments in Java passed by reference or by value?
A: Java is strictly pass-by-value (copies of primitives or copies of references are passed).
Q: What keyword indicates a method belongs to the class itself rather than instances?
A: static.
sections.common_mistakes:
- Attempting to call non-static methods directly from static `main`.
- Forgetting a `return` statement along a code branch.
sections.recap:
- Methods modularize and reuse code.
- Overloading differentiates methods by signature.

lessons.title: Arrays and Strings

sections.objectives:
- Declare, allocate, and index fixed-size arrays.
- Inspect array `.length`.
- Utilize common String manipulation methods.
sections.explanation:
Arrays are fixed-length sequences of elements of the same type:
```java
int[] numbers = new int[5]; // default initialized to 0
int[] primes = {2, 3, 5, 7, 11};
System.out.println(primes[0]); // 2
System.out.println(primes.length); // 5
```

Accessing indices outside `0` to `length - 1` throws `ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException`.

Strings provide rich inspection methods:
- `.length()`: number of characters
- `.charAt(index)`: character at index
- `.substring(start, end)`: sliced substring
- `.contains(seq)`, `.toUpperCase()`, `.toLowerCase()`
sections.knowledge_checks:
Q: What property gives the number of elements in an array?
A: .length (notice: no parentheses, unlike String.length()).
Q: What exception is thrown when an invalid array index is accessed?
A: ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException.
Q: Are Java Strings mutable?
A: No, Java Strings are immutable; methods like toUpperCase() return new Strings.
sections.common_mistakes:
- Writing `array.length()` with parentheses.
- Modifying a string and forgetting to reassign the result (`str.toUpperCase()` without `str = ...`).
sections.recap:
- Arrays are fixed-size and 0-indexed.
- Strings are immutable objects.

lessons.title: Classes and Objects

sections.objectives:
- Define classes with fields and constructors.
- Instantiate objects using `new`.
- Override the `toString()` method.
sections.knowledge_checks:
Q: What keyword allocates memory for a new object in Java?
A: new.
Q: What is the purpose of this keyword?
A: It references the current instance of the class.
Q: What method should you override to provide a custom string representation of an object?
A: public String toString().
sections.common_mistakes:
- Calling methods on an uninitialized reference, producing `NullPointerException`.
- Forgetting `this.` when constructor parameters shadow field names.
sections.recap:
- Classes encapsulate state (fields) and behavior (methods).
- `new` creates object instances.

checks.answer: new.

checks.answer: It references the current instance of the class.

lessons.title: Encapsulation

sections.objectives:
- Protect object integrity using `private` fields.
- Provide controlled access with getters and setters.
- Understand visibility modifiers.
sections.knowledge_checks:
Q: Why are fields usually declared private?
A: To prevent outside code from directly altering internal state into an invalid condition.
Q: What naming convention is used for getter methods in Java?
A: getFieldName() or isFieldName() for booleans.
Q: What is encapsulation?
A: Bundling data and behavior while restricting direct access to internal implementation details.
sections.common_mistakes:
- Making all fields public for convenience, breaking encapsulation guarantees.
- Not validating inputs in setters.
sections.recap:
- Keep fields `private`.
- Provide read/write access via `getters` and `setters`.

lessons.title: Collections

sections.objectives:
- Use dynamic lists with `java.util.ArrayList`.
- Store key-value mappings with `java.util.HashMap`.
- Iterate through collections.
sections.knowledge_checks:
Q: How does ArrayList differ from a regular array?
A: ArrayList can dynamically grow and shrink; regular arrays have fixed capacity.
Q: Can primitive types like int be directly stored in an ArrayList?
A: No, collections store objects; Java automatically boxes primitives into wrapper types like Integer.
Q: Which method checks if a key exists in a HashMap?
A: containsKey(key).
sections.common_mistakes:
- Writing `ArrayList<int>` instead of `ArrayList<Integer>`.
- Using `.length` instead of `.size()` on collections.
sections.recap:
- `ArrayList` provides dynamic array functionality.
- `HashMap` provides fast O(1) average lookup by key.

lessons.title: Exceptions and Error Handling

sections.objectives:
- Handle errors with `try`, `catch`, and `finally`.
- Throw exceptions with `throw`.
- Distinguish checked vs unchecked exceptions.
sections.knowledge_checks:
Q: Does a finally block execute if an exception occurs?
A: Yes, finally blocks always execute regardless of whether an exception was thrown or caught.
Q: What is the base class for exceptions that do not require mandatory handling?
A: RuntimeException (unchecked exceptions).
Q: What keyword is used to explicitly raise an exception?
A: throw.
sections.common_mistakes:
- Catching generic `Exception` and swallowing it silently without logging or handling.
- Forgetting that `finally` runs even if a `return` statement is hit inside `try`.
sections.recap:
- `try-catch` prevents crashes and handles errors gracefully.
- `finally` ensures cleanup runs.

projects.title: Bank Account & Transaction Simulator
projects.purpose: Master Java OOP fundamentals, encapsulation, defensive validation, and Scanner interaction.

milestones.title: BankAccount encapsulation
milestones.requirements: Create BankAccount with private accountNumber, holderName, and balance. Reject negative deposits or withdrawals exceeding balance.
acceptance_criteria: Validates positive deposit amounts
Withdrawal checks sufficient funds and returns boolean success
Balance can only be mutated through deposit/withdraw methods
milestones.hint: Check if (amount <= 0) return false; before modifying balance.

milestones.title: Transaction history recording
milestones.requirements: Track an ArrayList of Transaction objects with timestamp, type (DEPOSIT/WITHDRAW), and resulting balance.
acceptance_criteria: Every successful mutation appends a Transaction record
Provides printStatement() method formatting transactions
Protects history from external modification
milestones.hint: Return new ArrayList<>(transactions) in getTransactions() to prevent outside mutations.

milestones.title: Interactive Console Menu
milestones.requirements: Provide a loop offering deposit, withdraw, check balance, and statement options via Scanner.
acceptance_criteria: Loop continues until exit option is chosen
Handles invalid menu choice with polite notice
Maintains account state throughout user session
milestones.hint: Use a switch (choice) block inside while (!exit).

extensions: Support multiple accounts with account lookup by ID
Add interest calculation for savings accounts
Persist account records to a local text file

projects.title: Thread-Safe In-Memory Cache & Server

acceptance_criteria: Uses ConcurrentHashMap or ReadWriteLock for thread safety
Expired keys return null and are lazily or eagerly pruned

comparisons.same: Both languages run compiled object-oriented code with classes and methods.
different: Java runs in the JVM with an automatic Garbage Collector (GC); objects created with `new` are freed when unreachable.
C++ uses deterministic lifetime (RAII, destructors, smart pointers) and direct memory management without a GC pause.
Java has no pointers or manual `delete`, preventing memory leaks from forgotten frees, but gives up deterministic destruction order.
